A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoSketch work and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. The original 60-sketch gallery is retained with matching images and instructions; the added supplementary evaluations can be reliably distinguished.

before.justification: v1 reports original animation experiments, quantitative baseline comparisons in Table 2, and component ablations in Table 3, alongside qualitative results and failure cases.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds quantitative freehand and single-object evaluations in Tables 4–5, plus additional qualitative results.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.1 changes the stated decomposition limits from fewer than seven objects and five instructions to at most seven and five. The four-component pipeline otherwise remains intact. Renaming motion refinement, specifying Transformer details, and expanding the sub-video extraction description do not establish an architectural redesign.

E1.justification: Section S1 adds evaluation on human-drawn multi-object sketches from FS-COCO, extending coverage beyond the original image-derived sketches to imperfect freehand inputs. The original 60 sketches remain unchanged. Single-object animation was already demonstrated in v1 and is expanded, rather than newly introduced.

E2.justification: The retained single-object evaluation expands from MoSketch-only illustrations in v1 Figure 8 to comparisons with FlipSketch and Live-Sketch in v2 Table 5. The four comparators in the main Table 2 remain unchanged; CogVideoX and DynamiCrafter receive spelling corrections.

E3.justification: v2 specifies a selected 30-drawing FS-COCO test subset and introduces four-metric quantitative evaluation for the previously qualitative single-object scenario. The original 60-sketch evaluation, metrics, 16-frame outputs, 500 optimization steps, and optimizer settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Qualitative component ablations expand from the cannon example in v1 Figure 10 to cannon, eating, and basketball examples in v2 Figure 7, exposing additional interaction and refinement failures. Section S1 also tests external validity on imperfect freehand inputs. The quantitative ablations and three original failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added tables continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain identical numerical results, but v2 adds Tables 4–5 and substantial qualitative evidence. On freehand sketches, MoSketch reports 0.197 text alignment, 0.927 sketch alignment, 0.940 smoothness, and 0.633 dynamic degree. On single-object sketches, its text alignment is 0.209 versus Live-Sketch's 0.217 and FlipSketch's 0.211, while its smoothness is highest at 0.968.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theorems or proofs. The mathematical formulation is substantively retained: Equation 8 makes the already-described object-specific point extraction explicit, while other equation edits mainly change notation or presentation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: training-data-free multi-object animation through SDS, four cooperating modules, and superiority over existing sketch-animation approaches. The revised terminology and added supporting evaluations do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes large single-object displacements; v2 Section S2 adds an explicit qualification that MoSketch is less effective in that scenario, supported by mixed metric rankings. Section S1 interprets freehand results as improving drawing imperfections. Section 4.1 generalizes the alignment-metric bias already noted for ablations in v1 Table 3.

D1.justification: Section S3 supplies the actual instructions and input/output formats for both core GPT-4 stages, including bounding-box coordinates, a 256-by-256 image space, and planning constraints. Section 3.2.3 additionally specifies embedding concatenation, self-attention, and sketch positional encodings. A project-page URL replaces the earlier code-release promise, although the PDFs alone do not establish available repository contents.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FS-COCO and Transformer-based stroke relation encoding, connecting the new evaluation and implementation explanation to prior work. The existing related-work categories and positioning relative to Live-Sketch, FlipSketch, and compositional generation remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 edits introductory and related-work prose, standardizes method names, renames the refinement module, and clarifies compositional SDS. It folds the separate Results subsection into Section 4.1 and introduces organized supplementary sections S1–S3. The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The display organization changes substantially: v1 Figures 3–5 become the three panels of v2 Figure 3, the ablation display becomes a three-case grid, and single-object illustrations move to the supplement and expand. v2 also adds Tables 4–5 and supplementary result figures. The original sketch gallery is retained with revised captions.

improvement.justification: v2 improves external-validity evidence through the freehand evaluation, makes the single-object applicability discussion more balanced, and materially improves reproducibility by providing both GPT-4 instruction templates. These are useful, targeted gains. The added validation remains limited: the freehand test uses 30 drawings and the single-object test size is unspecified, while the main benchmark and quantitative ablation evidence remain unchanged.
